prompt:
You maintain a running summary of a long engineering document that is being read part by part, so that a later reader can model the system in SysML v2 without seeing the earlier parts.
Update the summary with the new part. Keep, as compactly as possible: the full names of system elements, actors and items; every alias or call sign with the full name it stands for; which element produces, sends or receives which item; modes and normative requirements. At most 300 words.

Current summary:
Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps) implements Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidance. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), airspace users, aircraft, pilots, controllers, traffic managers and automation participate within National Airspace System (NAS).
MBT covers all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft, including commercial aviation, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles and on-demand transportation. FAA/users negotiate assigned closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs), current-state-to-destination, respecting user goals/constraints. Aircraft must comply; pilots/controllers use compliance automation. Tolerances reflect performance/situation. Controllers retain separation/conflict-avoidance responsibility; IFR self-separation is not the far-term norm.
NAS Constraint Service publishes static/dynamic constraints. Traffic management automation translates traffic management initiatives (TMIs) into flight-specific constraints traceable to NAS constraints. Publish trajectory changes to relevant users, aircraft and FAA automation; aircraft share/update predicted 4DT intent. Traffic managers amend trajectories; all decisions consider downstream effects. Proactively resolve conflicts; minimize open vectoring using closed tactical modifications.
Digital air-ground communications deliver cockpit 4DTs for Flight Management System (FMS) execution. Broadband/electronic flight bag (EFB) applications support negotiation. Negotiating controller subsumes D-side responsibilities; traffic management coordinators (TMCs) support conflict avoidance/traffic flow management (TFM). Automation coordinates multisector changes.
Far-term encompasses all NAS air traffic control (ATC), assumes future enablers and widespread Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2). Near-term permits limited TBO, constrained by current NAS/planned NextGen NAS Enterprise Architecture (EA) evolution. Equipage follows safety/performance progression; highly equipped capabilities remain unchanged: Required Time of Arrival (RTA) FMS supports one active RTA. Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) supports route clearances/trajectory-intent output.
Introduce MBT incrementally through existing automation upgrades/System Wide Information Management (SWIM) extensions. Mixed equipage benefits; adoption varies by facility/controller; user technology adoption maintains current pace. Experience refines tools/acceptance; critical mass increases benefits.
Time-based performance complements Performance Based Navigation (PBN); time of arrival control (TOAC) certification thresholds risk mixed-equipage separation/unacceptable risk.

New part:
U0067: Equipped aircraft from participating operators will benefit from the ability to negotiate their trajectories and will be more likely to be left alone to follow the assigned trajectory.  Current structured airspace will remain in use, although increased use of direct routing will be allowed in regions of low-to-medium operational density.  Controllers will use automation support to define and issue closed trajectories in advance, rather than reverting to open-trajectory vectors issued via voice. 1.5.2 Assumptions about the Far-Term MBT Environment  EFBs will become much more capable and will have reliable, high-speed connectivity to ground-based systems.
U0068: This will enable a rapid advance in air vehicle capabilities without requiring all of the changes to occur within legacy FMS architectures, which could be more expensive and slower to enter the fleet.  All aircraft will be capable of receiving assigned trajectories via digital communication and flying these trajectories with known accuracies.
U0069: Voice will continue to exist for cases when immediate feedback and action are required.
U0070: While many aircraft will be capable of digitally receiving trajectories and automatically loading them into the FMS, others will require pilots to manually load trajectory data into the FMS or otherwise fly the assigned trajectory.  The rapid advance of technologies and applications for unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) operations in the NAS will overflow into other categories of aviation operations.
U0071: Current Traffic Collision Avoidance System/Airborne Collision Avoidance System (TCAS/ACAS) technology will experience a substantial evolution based on emerging UAS detect and avoid capabilities.
U0072: This technology change will converge with technologies that support self-separation between aircraft (e.g., Advanced Interval Management [A-IM]).
U0073: As a result, the long-term environment will be characterized by all IFR aircraft being equipped with coordinated tactical conflict avoidance capabilities that can detect and safely avoid complex conflict scenarios involving multiple aircraft of all types, while providing the planned avoidance maneuvers to ground automation via broadband communication.
U0074: This will provide the final layer of safety in the MBT concept.  TFM will evolve considerably.
U0075: GDPs and AFPs will move toward controlling by CTA at the constrained NAS resource rather than departure time.

Return JSON {"summary": "..."}.

Aircraft must comply within performance/situation-dependent tolerances; aircraft share predicted intent. Controllers retain separation/conflict-avoidance responsibility; routine IFR self-separation is not assumed.
